title: “To Save Our Brethren”: Mormons, Armenians, and the “Eastern Zion” in Ottoman Palestine and Beyond
abstract: On October 13, 1897, Mormon church leaders reached a consensus to establish a “colony in Palestine.”1 It was a major decision. After thirteen years of missionary work, some two hundred Armenian adults and children had congregated in four branches in Aleppo (northern Syria), Aintab and Marash (southern Turkey), and Zara (east-central Turkey). These converts faced daily, intense persecution in their homeland due to their conversion to an “alien” faith. They were thwarted from emigrating to be with the Saints in America because of their poverty and the hostility of both American and Ottoman officials. In view of the desperate straits of these Armenian Mormons, the church leaders proposed an “Eastern Zion.” They dispatched a high-level delegation, including Apostle Anthon Lund, former Turkish Mission President Ferdinand Hintze, and Hagop Gagosian, an Armenian convert who had emigrated from Turkey to Utah, to determine a site for an agricultural colony, negotiate terms for the purchase of land, obtain formal permission for the gathering and resettlement of the Armenian congregations, and offer an apostolic benediction on the land.2The envoys left Utah on January 6, 1898, visiting Mormon communities and missionaries in the eastern United States and Europe. They debarked at Jaffa, in Ottoman Palestine on February 17, 1898.3 Phillip Maycock and Andrew Larson, the two missionaries then working in the Turkish Mission, greeted them. Together, the members of the delegation began their work.Though the number of Armenian Saints was small compared to other Mormon missionary fields, the story of the 1898 Mormon delegation provides important information to understand deeply held beliefs about time, place, and peoples at a pivotal moment in the church's history. The story also reveals the lengths significant religious actors would go to reshape doctrinal beliefs and attitudes to assist a beleaguered community of fellow church members in a distant empire.To determine how to set up a colony, the Mormon delegation explored similar settlements in Ottoman Palestine. The first day, they visited the German “Templer settlement.” A small evangelical German Lutheran group, inspired by their reading of biblical prophetic passages, the Templers had started a “perfect” Christian community in Haifa in preparation for Christ's Second Coming. The Mormon group then took the land route northward toward Haifa. They stopped at the Jewish settlements of Haderah and “Sammarin” (Zikhron Ya'akov) to examine agricultural efforts. In Haderah, the Mormons met with Selig Soskin, a Russian-born, German-trained agronomist who had emigrated to Palestine two years earlier and was working for the Palestine Executive of the Odessa Committee of Hovevei Zion.4 Lund reported obtaining “much valuable information” from “the Doctor” on land reclamation, property and produce taxes, livestock and cereals, and eucalyptus tree planting as an anti-malarial measure. He was “glad to have taken that route,” visiting “the Jewish colonies” and learning from Soskin “considerable information in regard to what they had done and the resources of the country.”5 The group then visited the “American colony” in Jerusalem. Founded by Horatio and Anna Spafford in 1881, there were 150 American and Swedish members by 1896 dedicated to non-proselytizing, philanthropic work in Jerusalem. Lund praised their cooperative spirit. These settlements played a key role in making Mormon arguments for a “colony” of Armenian Saints plausible.Earlier Mormon missionaries had visited other colony settlements from 1884 to 1898 while touring throughout Palestine. They “traveled from colony to colony”—both Jewish and Christian—and, in some cases, published extensive descriptions of their experiences.6 For example, Danish convert and missionary Janne Sjodahl wrote articles for the Deseret News Weekly divided into sections entitled “Objects of Jewish Colonization,” “Colonization Methods,” “Colonial Life,” “Religious Notions and Education,” and “Non-Colonizing Jews.”7 He compared Jewish and “Gentile” agricultural colonies and noted the transitions underway in Jewish settlements. He remarked on the “inviting appearance” of Petah Tikveh, Rosh Pinah, and “Samarin” (Zikhron Ya'akov), observing: “It is very pleasing to me to note . . . on the progress everywhere going on. . . . The Jews are settling to stay.”8Sjodahl and other Mormon missionaries noted the number of settlers, the types and arrangementsof buildings, enterprises, crops, livestock, and cultivation methods. Sjodahl explained, “These people have fully demonstrated what diligence and skill can do here. They have bought up some desert lands . . . have terraced mountains . . . laid out the land in vineyards, and they are obtaining fair returns from their labor.”9 These descriptions and assessments helped the 1898 delegates lay out plans for establishing a Mormon colony. They also contributed to the Mormons’ positive regard for modern Zionist settlements and ideology during the Ottoman and British Mandate periods.10Those who wrote these descriptions of potential Palestine settlements drew upon their experiences in Utah. In the last decades of the nineteenth century, Mormon leaders remained keen proponents of agricultural colonization efforts carried out by church members for economic, social, and cultural reasons.11 The proposal to settle urban Armenians alongside a small number of European and American Mormons assigned by church headquarters to colonize according to up-to-date agrarian and industrial skills drew upon longstanding experience in the American West; it also rose from deep seated convictions about the necessity for the in-gathering of the Saints before the “coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord.”12With this background, Hintze and other missionaries sought official recognition (millet status) for the Mormon community in Ottoman domains.13 They met with U.S. and European consular agents for advice and information,14 consulted with Armenian converts,15 and upon returning to Mormon church headquarters in Utah, met with church leaders to enlist their support.16After visiting colony examples, Lund and the rest of the delegation traveled by steamship, carriage, and horseback to Aintab (Gaziantep), Turkey, site of the largest Mormon Armenian community, in March 1898.17 Lund's delegation ministered to the Saints for a month. They viewed and heard first-hand graphic examples of faithfulness and of anxieties, of the indigence of church members and the indignities imposed on those who converted to the new religion. For example, members recollected how “they had a hard time finding work because they were Mormons. [We] were the first ones fired and the last ones hired.” “We tried to hold meetings, which was difficult,” said George Z. Aposhian, “but we held them for several years. As members, we would go to church [and] people would stand on the side of the road and throw sticks and stones. . . . This went on for quite some time.”18The delegation then held two major council sessions to introduce the proposed colony. Most members, however, preferred emigrating to Utah. But they recognized the American and Ottoman travel restrictions, as well as their own poverty as prohibitive. So the delegation persuaded them to back the colony scheme. However, the Armenian Saints insisted that “light industry”—that is, weaving and rug making—be an essential part of the colony plan since most of the male church members were weavers, dyers, and rug makers and not experienced farmers. Moses Hindoian, of the Aintab branch, for example, “made his living by spinning and weaving wool. Everyone helped, even the children. So [his son] Abraham started working with wool . . . in his early years.”19 The Armenians also advised the Americans on prudent land purchase approaches and securing ownership titles.20After these meetings, the delegation traveled through “all the principal part of Palestine”21 in April and May 1898. During this period, they met with American consular officials in Beirut and Jerusalem, Turkish and Arab landowners and their agents, and German and Jewish settlers. They visited historic sites and surveyed a number of properties available for purchase. While they discussed sites near Nablus and Jericho as possessing great potential for agricultural settlement,22 it was the property near Haifa owned by Selim Khouri, a businessman and sometimes Russian and Greek charge d’ affaires, that seized their interest.23 It was a six thousand acre site about fifteen miles southeast of Haifa—the village and land of “El Kireh.” Though Khouri's asking price was $120,000, the envoys recommended it to general church officials in Utah for purchase and settlement.24The delegation's accounts matched historical geographer Ruth Kark's observations about “trends and processes connected with land and settlement” during this period.25 Mormons noted “the long term neglect” of once fertile and populated lands.26 They reported extensive tracts available for purchase by foreigners.27 They worried about the unsettled nature of occupancy rights versus land titles possessed and sold by absentee landowners.28 Discussions between Mormons, American consuls, and land agents show that Ottoman officials and merchant families in Beirut and Jaffa were deeply involved in speculative land ownership and that many of them sought avidly to realize profits on land sales to foreign buyers.29The Mormons were also part of a trend in the late 1880s and 1890s. Overriding ideological, rather than entrepreneurial, interest motivated land purchase and settlement in Ottoman Palestine.30 The delegation were there to “see our Zion . . . here” and save their Armenian fellow Saints.31 They feared displacing fellahin from Khouri's lands and occasionally asked “where the Son of man has been.”32 The goal of the Mormon colony was to create an economically self-sustaining refuge for the Saints, an enclave of “true arts” and “civilization” which would serve as a refuge from persecution and, in the interim, as a “city on the hill in the ‘East,’” even as Mormons hoped their settlement in the semi-arid valleys of the Rocky Mountains would serve as a sanctuary in the “latter-days” before the Lord's Second Advent.Land agents and owners told the Mormons repeatedly that they “could get anything they wanted” in the way of property, and in “any amount,” even if it meant driving its inhabitants off the land. This showed the uncertainties of the Ottoman agrarian classes and the impunity of their overlord's use of power.33 The Mormon delegation observed tax conscriptees working fitfully and fruitlessly on a road project that led nowhere. title: Sanford Levinson, Review of Yasuo Hasebe, Towards a Normal Constitutional State: The Trajectory of Japanese Constitutionalism
abstract: This thought-provoking book invites at least three quite different modes of review. Although the title refers to “Japanese constitutionalism,” that is only one aspect of the book, and at least to some readers it may not be the most important one. Much of the book’s discussion of what counts as a “normal constitutional state” in fact involves stimulating and challenging discussions of general jurisprudence that will interest all international participants in the relevant debates. Finally, there are some distinctly comparative aspects to the book, particularly an illuminating chapter on war powers in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Japan. In my own case, as I accepted the invitation to review the book hoping to deepen my limited knowledge of Japanese constitutionalism, which in fact resulted, I found myself most caught up in the first aspect of the book. I will, however, try to offer a fair overview of what is obviously a rich book that can profitably be read by a variety of audiences throughout the world. Professor Hasebe, who is professor of constitutional law at Waseda Law School and an emeritus professor at the University of Tokyo, makes it very clear at the outset that for him a “normal constitutional state” is one committed to what we should call “liberal constitutionalism.” Like Dieter Grimm,1 Hasebe believes that a “proper” (and therefore normal) constitutional order will be committed to preserving some genuine degree of individual liberty and will, in addition, be careful to place restraints on state power. Not the least reason for his commitment is his reiterated emphasis on the ineluctable pluralism of what John Rawls called “comprehensive views” of how to order life and society, with the concomitant need to construct an approach to constitutional order that allows pluralism to flourish. Thus, the book almost literally begins with a reference to “ensur[ing] the fair coexistence in society of various incommensurable world views” in a manner that will “successfully combine universal freedom and social stability” (at 1). He thus announces at the outset his suspicion of anyone committed to a strong notion of “constitutional identity” inasmuch as that “means overlooking the principles of modern constitutionalism” (id.), which suggests precisely the existence of groups with competing identities—and, perhaps, definitions of what they might think to be preferred constitutional projects—who must learn to live with one another. Not surprisingly in this context, the final of the book’s twenty chapters, though labeled an “afterword,” asks “What is the Constitutional Identity of Japan?” His answer, basically, Is that one cannot answer that question coherently, because there is no singular identity “inherent to [modern] Japan” (at 340). He does not rue this, because the alternative would give succor to modern-day nationalists, who do use a particularly constitutionalized form of “identity politics” as a means of vindicating what has come to be called “illiberal constitutionalism.” Hasebe is obviously aware of Gary Jacobsohn’s important book Constitutional Identity (2010), and he might accept Jacobsohn’s insights as empirically important, even as he warns against treating any particularistic notion of identity (other, presumably, than a commitment to pluralistic liberal constitutionalism) as normative. His particular discussion and concerns may be based on Japanese history, especially since World War II, but it is obvious that his qualms go far beyond that particular country. Jacobsohn himself has written eloquently and critically about recent developments in two countries he has examined extensively: India and Israel. Whatever the liberal democratic aspirations of many of their founders in the 1940s, who were largely secular in orientation and wished to create basically secular states, both countries have in effect been politically conquered by distinctly nationalist movements founded on religious identity, whether Hindu, as in India, or Jewish, as in Israel. Pluralism is taking a back seat in relation to modern forms of integralism. As Ran Hirschl and Li-Ann Thio have reminded us,2 “our” distaste for such regimes does not negate their realities or allow us to ignore them because “we,” as secular pluralists, find them justifiably distasteful. There is a reason, after all, why the Routledge Handbook of Illiberalism has just been published with sixty-one essays over almost a thousand pages, many of them inevitably touching on topics relating to law and constitutionalism.3 Modern theories of constitutional identity may be rooted in the ostensible implications of what is surely the most pervasive general political theory since the seventeenth century: “popular sovereignty.” If one takes seriously the notion, which perhaps received its canonical twentieth-century articulation in Woodrow Wilson’s commitment to “national self-determination,”4 then one will posit the existence of some unique “people” who can legitimately exercise their “sovereignty” in order to structure a highly particularistic nation-state. That almost inevitably creates a binary understanding of “insiders,” who are part of the demos, and “outsiders,” who, even if not out-and-out Schmittian “enemies,” are nonetheless not included within the constitutional order or are merely “tolerated” rather than genuinely embraced. After all, the United States Declaration of Independence begins with the astonishing assertion that in British North America there is “one people” that is entitled in effect to secede from the British Empire and to create their (or should it be “its”) own government rooted in some notion of particularistic “consent.” Similarly, the US Constitution begins with an evocation of “We the People,” rather than the sociologically more accurate “peoples.” As David Armitage has well argued,5 it is that feature of the Declaration, far more than the articulation of “inalienable rights,” that, especially when reinterpreted by Wilson, has been of genuinely world-historical importance, accompanied by both inspiration and almost endless turmoil. As many people have noted, there are too many “peoples” with claims to “nationhood” and not enough land to provide the territory in which they can enjoy the “self-determination” they seek. But the allure of “national self-determination” remains strong. I have frequently quoted the astonishing paragraph in The Federalist No. 2, written by John Jay, in which he takes “notice that Providence has been pleased” to settle the New World with “one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs….” Perhaps borrowing from Montesquieu, Jay seems to be suggesting that what the Constitution terms a “republican form of government” requires, if not necessarily a small territory, then at least, and more importantly, a homogeneous society sharing “the same principles of government” and united behind a common constitutional project. In the case of the United States, this required Jay simply to profess ignorance of the most obvious dissonances within his own state of New York, including racialized chattel slavery that existed until 1827 and a number of indigenous nations living on ancestral lands throughout the state. His observation about New Yorkers “speaking the same language” was belied by the fact that the Constitution proposed in September 1787 was quickly translated into Dutch so that the Dutch speakers living north of Manhattan could understand it and debate whether it should be ratified. (It was also translated into German for the benefit of the roughly one-third of Pennsylvanians for whom that was their primary language.) But, of course, the United States may be in fact “exceptional” with regard to the degree of its pluralism that was present even at the creation, whether or not fully acknowledged and grappled with. More “normal,” in at least some ways, may be countries like Japan, which tenaciously protect a highly particularistic notion of national identity and appear resistant to any genuine sense of pluralism beyond, perhaps, the value pluralism that Hasebe refers to and embraces.6 But, quite obviously, whatever its importance, it does not capture the quite different pluralism that is represented by multiple groups divided by ethnicity, race, or religion (which might, of course, translate itself into conflicting value commitments as well, especially if, for example, proponents of given religions claim a right to be exempt from obeying certain laws passed by the state). I wish that Hasebe had devoted at least a chapter to considering Japan’s own policies, constitutional and otherwise, concerning immigration and citizenship. These are issues that go well beyond theoretical interest; Japan looms especially prominent among countries that appear to be losing population because of a declining birth rate, with significant consequences for the entire social and economic order. For starters, there are ever more elderly Japanese, who may be very much in need of the kind of services that immigrants might be willing to provide. Unless Japan relaxes its traditional reluctance to welcome those considered strangers, what will the future be for now middle-aged Japanese nationals, among many others? But, of course, a traditional attribute of “sovereignty” associated with “national self-determination” is precisely the right to build walls and lift drawbridges in an effort to maintain what may be described, from within, as the maintenance of social (or even “constitutional”) identity. That is, after all, what is often implied in the notion of nationhood itself. It would certainly be unfair to suggest that only Japan is faced with the tension between demographic realities and maintaining certain notions of national identity. But it certainly presents one of the most obvious examples of a both literal and metaphorical insularity that is in tension with what many would define as cosmopolitan pluralism. Hasebe announces his refreshing desire to simply end the traditional discourse that emphasizes “sovereignty,” popular or otherwise, as the basis for the legitimacy of any given constitutional order (including Japan’s). Chapter One is titled, forthrightly, “Why We Should Not Take the Sovereignty Too Seriously.” One might read this together with Don Herzog’s bracing Sovereignty, RIP (2020), which suggests that the concept has long since outlasted its theoretical utility, rooted as it is in theories offered to end the bloody religious wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. It is fitting that Hasebe’s first chapter is followed by two chapters indicating his disdain for the very important concept, at last for popular sovereignty enthusiasts, of constituent power and the associated search for a knowable “rule of recognition” that gives legitimacy to the constitutional enterprise. If God no longer provides the basis for rule—the dominant view at least in the West since the seventeenth century—then what does? The answer for many, of course, is “We the People.” This need not, of course, mean that “the people” rule directly; indeed, as Hobbes argued, “authorization” is the heart of the matter, and “the people” have the privilege to decide that a monarch would be desirable. Perhaps this helps to understand the Japanese belief that some valuable function is served by an emperor, even if he (or, in the future, she) is no longer viewed as in fact divine. It remains telling that one of the most important conflicts between Japan and the American victors at the conclusion of World War II concerned whether the emperor should be retained at all, let alone continuing to assert his divine status. General MacArthur capitulated on the former; the Japanese on the latter. It is unclear how actually important the emperor is in understanding the functioning Japanese polity; one might make the same point about the House of Windsor in contemporary Great Britain. Yet, in both societies, what one might think of as “the republican imperative” appears to be absent, for better or worse. Still, there appears to be a desire, even if not shared by Hasebe, to trace the foundation of the Japanese constitutional order—even one with an emperor at its helm—to a seeming decision by “the people” to establish the polity, its basic norms, and institutions. But why? For Hasebe, what constitutes a “normal constitutional state” is not at all that its legitimacy can be traced to some singular act of a sovereign founder (or group of such founders authorized, in some mysterious way, to speak on behalf of “the people”); instead, what is key is the existence of a set of “customary practice[s] shared among judges, public officials and private persons who are in charge of applying rules recognized as valid in the legal system” (at 41). Such practices are “matter[s] of fact” and not grand theory (id.). As he puts it later in the book, “practice, not texts, generate constitutional law” (at 313, emphasis in original). Sociology takes precedence over jurisprudence and political theory. Perhaps one might suggest that a test of “normality” is precisely that, save for basically (and blessedly) marginalized academics, there is no serious discussion of what does indeed justify the given order, because all important actors simply accept it as a given and continue to go about their daily lives. This is the view adopted by my colleague Philip Bobbitt,7 who completely separates the questions of how or why particular legal answers are deemed true—or acceptable—from any questions about the underlying legitimacy of the legal order itself. As a Wittgensteinian, Bobbitt appears to regard the question of legitimacy as illustrating a kind of philosophical pathology, and therefore one to be excised from our thought. But, of course, such a “foundational” question is in fact hard to excise.
